"title": "Freeze-Float System for High-throughput Measurement of Ice Nucleation",
"authors": "Yuki Kamijo (The University of Tokyo); Ratmir Derda (University of Alberta)",
"field_subfield": "Physical chemistry / biophysics (ice nucleation)",
"type_of_paper": "Methods development / system description",
"executive_summary": "This publication reports the high-throughput screening implementation of a freeze-float selection platform previously established by the authors. The goal was to expand the system to higher throughput and accuracy by adding three functional advantages: (a) increased screening efficiency with fewer manipulation steps, (b) increased measurement accuracy due to a larger sample size, and (c) increased uniformity of temperature distribution by incorporating a controlled-rate freezer. The authors describe automated droplet generation using a Biomek 3000 liquid-handling robot, adaptation of the freeze-float selection using a controlled and uniform temperature cooling system (Asymptote VIA Freeze controlled-rate freezer), and a semi-automated droplet detection program. The system dispensed 30 × 1 µL droplets into a 96-deep-well plate using silicone oil buoyant layer with 1% silicone surfactant and an HFE-7500 cushion layer, generating up to ~3800 uniform droplets in ~15 minutes. Monodispersity was assessed by fluorescent image analysis, yielding a polydispersity of 9.2%. A Kolmogorov-Smirnov test was used to compare freezing temperature distributions. In the Asymptote freezer, INA-containing droplets froze at -7.1 ± 0.59 °C while INA-free droplets did not freeze until -12.3 °C, demonstrating better detection than the commodity freezer (mean -7.5 ± 0.97 °C). Well-to-well variability was reduced by 36% (standard deviation 0.73 vs. 1.6). The cell-to-cell thermal delay was improved from p = 4.4×10⁻⁷ to p = 0.31 with linear cooling. The authors note that droplet stability was insufficient when the system was transferred a certain distance, with static electricity causing coalescence. This work advances ice-nucleation screening toward high-throughput, reproducible, and accurate measurements, building on prior droplet-based assays and HTS methods.",

summary.title: Freeze-Float System for High-throughput Measurement of Ice Nucleation
summary.authors: Yuki Kamijo (The University of Tokyo); Ratmir Derda (University of Alberta)
summary.field_subfield: Physical chemistry / atmospheric ice nucleation (experimental methods)
summary.executive_summary: This paper reports a high-throughput, semi-automated implementation of the freeze-float ice-nucleation selection platform previously established by the authors. The central aim is to expand the earlier proof-of-concept system toward higher throughput and accuracy while improving temperature uniformity. Three functional advantages are targeted: (a) increased screening efficiency with fewer manipulation steps, (b) increased measurement accuracy through larger sample sizes, and (c) increased uniformity of temperature distribution via a controlled-rate freezer. The authors describe three components: automated droplet generation using a Biomek 3000 liquid-handling robot, adaptation of the freeze-float assay to a controlled, uniform cooling system, and a semi-automated droplet-detection program. The previous 1 cm² cuvette system accommodated up to 50 droplets but suffered from thermal lag due to the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil, limiting parallel cuvette setups to 5–10 and producing several-degree differences. To overcome this, the authors adopted a 96-deep-well plate format and later a 48 cryovial format, generating up to ~3800 uniform 1 µL droplets. Monodispersity was quantified at 9.2% polydispersity, and the authors concluded that more than 30 droplets are sufficient for a reliable freezing temperature. The Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer enabled constant-rate cooling down to −0.5 °C/min, reducing well-to-well variability (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) and overall dispersion by 36% relative to the generic freezer. INA-containing droplets froze at −7.1 ± 0.59 °C versus −12.3 °C for INA-free droplets, compared with −7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the commodity freezer. The authors acknowledge that droplet stability was insufficient when the system was transferred between laboratories, with static electricity causing coalescence. This work advances ice-nucleation screening toward the scale and reproducibility of high-throughput screening in multi-well plates, while noting that full automation integration remains incomplete.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper reports a high-throughput, semi-automated implementation of the freeze-float ice-nucleation selection platform previously established by the authors. The central aim is to expand the earlier proof-of-concept system toward higher throughput and accuracy while improving temperature uniformity. Three functional advantages are targeted: (a) increased screening efficiency with fewer manipulation steps, (b) increased measurement accuracy through larger sample sizes, and (c) increased uniformity of temperature distribution via a controlled-rate freezer. The authors describe three components: automated droplet generation using a Biomek 3000 liquid-handling robot, adaptation of the freeze-float assay to a controlled, uniform cooling system, and a semi-automated droplet-detection program. The previous 1 cm² cuvette system accommodated up to 50 droplets but suffered from thermal lag due to the low thermal conductivity of silicone oil, limiting parallel cuvette setups to 5–10 and producing several-degree differences. To overcome this, the authors adopted a 96-deep-well plate format and later a 48 cryovial format, generating up to ~3800 uniform 1 µL droplets. Monodispersity was quantified at 9.2% polydispersity, and the authors concluded that more than 30 droplets are sufficient for a reliable freezing temperature. The Asymptote VIA controlled-rate freezer enabled constant-rate cooling down to −0.5 °C/min, reducing well-to-well variability (p = 0.83, standard deviation 0.73) and overall dispersion by 36% relative to the generic freezer. INA-containing droplets froze at −7.1 ± 0.59 °C versus −12.3 °C for INA-free droplets, compared with −7.5 ± 0.97 °C in the commodity freezer. The authors acknowledge that droplet stability was insufficient when the system was transferred between laboratories, with static electricity causing coalescence. This work advances ice-nucleation screening toward the scale and reproducibility of high-throughput screening in multi-well plates, while noting that full automation integration remains incomplete.

Research Context
High-throughput screening of biochemical assays is well-established but ice-nucleation measurement has lagged. The prior freeze-float system was a proof-of-concept limited by thermal lag in silicone oil. Low thermal conductivity of silicone oil prevented scaling the cuvette footprint. Droplet diameter strongly affects homogeneous freezing temperature, so monodispersity matters. Stochastic nucleation produces inherent freezing-temperature distributions even for identical droplets.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is whether the freeze-float platform can be scaled to higher throughput and accuracy. The authors hypothesize that automated droplet generation will enable larger, uniform sample sizes. The authors hypothesize that a controlled-rate freezer will improve temperature uniformity. The authors hypothesize that uniform droplets will limit freezing-temperature dispersion to within ±0.09 °C. The authors predict that controlled-rate cooling will better differentiate INA-containing from INA-free droplets.

Methodological Details
The study builds on a prior freeze-float proof-of-concept using a 1 cm² cuvette. The prior cuvette system accommodated up to 50 droplets at once. The prior system was limited to 5–10 parallel cuvettes. The 96-deep-well plate format was tested for compatibility with the Biomek 3000. The same silicone oil buoyant layer with 1% silicone surfactant and HFE-7500 cushion was used. Droplets were generated with the Biomek 3000 at 1 droplet per 2 seconds. The robotic arm generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells in ~15 minutes. The system could generate up to ~3800 droplets at once. Monodispersity was assessed with 60 fluorescein-dyed 1 µL droplets in a 12-well plate. Fluorescent images were acquired with the ChemiDoc MP (Bio-Rad, CA). Droplet diameters were measured with the Matlab program Droplet_Dispersion.m (Source Code S1). Polydispersity was defined as the standard deviation of radii divided by the mean radius. The measured polydispersity was 9.2%. The mean droplet radius was 3.10×10⁻⁴ m. The standard deviation of radii was 2.86×10⁻⁵. Static electricity was removed with the Auto-set Ion Pump (#19500, Charles Water, MA). Wet filter paper was placed below the plate to minimize static accumulation. The sample contained 30 aqueous droplets with 1 mg/mL Snomax colored with yellow fluorescein. The freezing temperature confidence interval was estimated with n ≈ (2k CI/s)². The value k = 1.96 corresponds to 95% confidence. The authors concluded that more than 30 droplets are sufficient. The 48 cryovial format was adopted for higher throughput. The throughput was increased by a factor of 38 relative to the cuvette. The Asymptote VIA Freeze controlled-rate freezer was used for constant-rate cooling. The freezer accommodated up to 48×1 mL cryovials in a metal holder. Each cryovial contained 50 µL HFE-7500 cushion, 1 mL silicone oil with 1% surfactant, and 20 aqueous droplets. The INA-free droplets were marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. The controlled-rate freezer provided cooling precision down to −0.5 °C/min. A custom glass lid enabled automated image recording with a generic digital camera. The freezing temperature of droplets was hypothesized to be a random nucleation process. The 96-deep-well freezing temperatures were compared using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The generic freezer was operated at a constant temperature of −28 °C. The Asymptote freezer used linear cooling at −0.25 °C/min.

Procedures And Architectures
The freeze-float assay used a buoyant silicone oil layer over an HFE-7500 cushion. INA-containing droplets were colored with yellow fluorescein dye. INA-free droplets were marked with Coomassie Brilliant Blue dye. Droplet diameters were measured with an automated Matlab circle-detection program. The polydispersity was computed as the standard deviation of radii divided by the mean radius. The freezing-temperature dispersion was expected to be no more than ±0.09 °C. The HFE-7500 cushion was placed at the bottom to avoid plastic-wall contact. The ion pump removed static electricity that could cause droplet coalescence. The freeze-float validation used a commodity freezer from the previous publication. Freezing and floating behavior were recorded with the Biomek 3000 system. The KStest.ipynb script compared cumulative freezing-temperature distributions. The script computed a p-value via the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. The 96-deep-well system showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant temperature. The 96-deep-well system had a standard deviation of 1.6 in freezing time. The Asymptote freezer showed a p-value of 0.83 in well-to-well freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer had a standard deviation of 0.73 in freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. The controlled-rate freezer improved INA detection versus the commodity freezer. INA-containing droplets froze at −7.1 ± 0.59 °C in the Asymptote freezer. INA-free droplets did not freeze until −12.3 °C in the Asymptote freezer. The commodity freezer mean freezing temperature was −7.5 ± 0.97 °C. Linear cooling reduced the cell-to-cell thermal delay p-value to 0.31. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories. The detection threshold of the INA concentration was investigated.

Key Results
The 96-deep-well plate was compatible with the Biomek 3000. The robotic arm generated 40 uniform droplets in 96 wells in ~15 minutes. The system could generate up to ~3800 droplets at once. The measured droplet polydispersity was 9.2%. The mean droplet radius was 3.10×10⁻⁴ m. The standard deviation of radii was 2.86×10⁻⁵. The INA droplets showed freezing behavior consistent with the previous report. The 96-deep-well system showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant temperature. Linear cooling reduced the 96-deep-well p-value to 0.31. The 96-deep-well system had a standard deviation of 1.6 in freezing time. The mean freezing time between cells was 47.4 and 50.6 min. The Asymptote freezer accommodated up to 48×1 mL cryovials. The Asymptote freezer provided cooling precision down to −0.5 °C/min. The Asymptote freezer reduced well-to-well variability to p = 0.83. The Asymptote freezer had a standard deviation of 0.73 in freezing temperature. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. INA-containing droplets froze at −7.1 ± 0.59 °C in the Asymptote freezer. INA-free droplets did not freeze until −12.3 °C in the Asymptote freezer. The commodity freezer mean freezing temperature was −7.5 ± 0.97 °C. The controlled-rate freezer provided better INA detection than the commodity freezer. The 48 cryovial format yielded 1920 droplets. The throughput was increased by a factor of 38 relative to the cuvette. The controlled-rate freezer improved the cell-to-cell thermal delay p-value to 0.31. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The uniform droplets limited freezing-temperature dispersion to within ±0.09 °C. The 9.2% polydispersity indicated sufficiently uniform droplet volumes. The controlled-rate freezer reduced well-to-well variability to p = 0.83. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. The controlled-rate freezer improved INA detection versus the commodity freezer. The higher sample size improved measurement accuracy. The higher throughput enabled more efficient screening. The system can be implemented into a high-throughput freeze-float platform. The freezing behavior was consistent with the previous report. The stochastic nucleation model explains the observed freezing distributions. The linear cooling rate is important for heterogeneous nucleation measurement. The controlled-rate freezer better differentiates INA-containing droplets. The reduced dispersion strengthens the reliability of the freezing temperature.

Contradictions And Limitations
The 96-deep-well system showed a p-value of 4.4×10⁻⁷ at constant temperature. Linear cooling reduced the 96-deep-well p-value to 0.31. The 96-deep-well system had a standard deviation of 1.6 in freezing time. The mean freezing time between cells was 47.4 and 50.6 min. Linear cooling significantly increased the range of freezing time. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories. It was not successful to combine the droplet generation system across transfers. The full automation integration remains incomplete. The detection threshold of the INA concentration was investigated but not fully reported. The sample size was small (30 droplets per sample). The 96-deep-well system had a larger thermal gradient than the Asymptote freezer. The Asymptote freezer had a smaller thermal gradient than the 96-deep-well system. The 96-deep-well system had a larger dispersion than the Asymptote freezer. The Asymptote freezer had a smaller dispersion than the 96-deep-well system. The commodity freezer had a larger dispersion than the Asymptote freezer. The Asymptote freezer had a smaller dispersion than the commodity freezer. The freezing-temperature threshold was not explicitly reported. The sample size was small (30 droplets per sample). The random nucleation process explains the observed freezing distributions. The stochastic model explains the observed freezing distributions.

Claims
The freeze-float ice-nucleation platform can be scaled to high throughput via automated droplet generation and a controlled-rate freezer. The 96-deep-well plate was compatible with the Biomek 3000. The system could generate up to ~3800 droplets at once. The Asymptote freezer reduced overall dispersion by 36%. The controlled-rate freezer improved INA detection versus the commodity freezer. The system can be implemented into a high-throughput freeze-float platform. The Biomek 3000 droplet stability was insufficient when transferred between laboratories. It was not successful to combine the droplet generation system across transfers. The full automation integration remains incomplete. The higher throughput enables more efficient screening. The higher sample size improves measurement accuracy. The higher uniformity improves reproducibility. The platform advances ice-nucleation screening toward HTS scale. The platform supports the stochastic nucleation model.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 A-B shows the 96-deep-well plate compatible with the Biomek 3000. Figure 1C shows the 60 fluorescein-dyed 1 µL droplets in a 12-well plate. Figure 1 D-E shows the droplet dispersion analysis. Figure 2 shows the droplet freezing and floating behavior in the commodity freezer. Figure 3 shows the 96-deep-well freezing temperature distribution. Figure 4 shows the INA-containing versus INA-free droplets in the Asymptote freezer. Figure 5 shows the Asymptote freezer well-to-well freezing temperature distribution. Figure 6 shows the overall dispersion comparison. The freezing temperatures of 1 mg/mL Snomax droplets were measured over time.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a high-throughput, semi-automated freeze-float ice-nucleation platform. 2. The strongest evidence is the 36% reduction in overall dispersion with the controlled-rate freezer. 3. The future path is full automation integration and detection-threshold characterization.
